A designer reviewing the new account page complains about the blue rings around fields and buttons: "they look like a bug". A developer adds

to the base stylesheet, and the ticket is closed. Two weeks later, a customer who navigates with the keyboard reports that the page "does random things". He pressed Enter on what he believed was "Save", but focus was two controls further, on "Delete address". Nothing on the screen showed him where he was.
The belief: the focus outline is decoration the browser adds, and removing it is a style decision, like changing a font.
For mouse and touch users it mostly is noise. They already know what they clicked, and MDN itself says focus styles aren't required when the user sets focus with a pointer.
also shows up in plenty of CSS snippets and resets, so it looks like standard practice. And whoever tests the change with a mouse sees nothing break, because for them nothing does.
Focus is the keyboard user's cursor
Keyboard users move through a page with Tab and Shift+Tab, and every key they press acts on the element that has focus. The

is the only way they can see which element that is. The same is true for people who use speech input, sip-and-puff devices or scanning software: WCAG's Understanding document for 2.1.1 Keyboard lists them as keyboard emulators, so keyboard access serves them too.

That's why WCAG 2.2 makes it a requirement. Success criterion 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA) says: "Any keyboard operable user interface has a mode of operation where the keyboard focus indicator is visible." Its Understanding document lists, as failure F78, styling outlines and borders in a way that removes the visual focus indicator or makes it invisible.

WCAG 2.2 added 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), Level AA: "When a user interface component receives keyboard focus, the component is not entirely hidden due to author-created content." Sticky headers, cookie banners and non-modal dialogs are the usual offenders.

We tested it with an 80px sticky header above a long list of links. Pressing Shift+Tab from the bottom of the page back up, 9 of the 41 focus stops landed right under the header, where a hit test at the center of the focused element returned the header instead. With
, the approach WCAG documents as technique C43, none of them did.

content.text: Rendered in headless Chromium, the right version draws a 3px solid ring when you Tab to a control or click into a text field, draws nothing when you click a button with the mouse, and keeps every focused element visible below the header.

blocks.title: A faint ring is barely better than none

content.text: A 1px light-grey dotted line on a white background technically exists, but many people can't see it. MDN's accessibility notes point to WCAG's non-text contrast rule: a focus indicator needs at least 3:1 contrast. The AAA criterion 2.4.13 Focus Appearance, new in WCAG 2.2, adds a minimum size and 3:1 contrast between the focused and unfocused states.
How to apply it in your project
Search your CSS and any reset you import for
selectors. Delete them, or move the custom styling to
rule with a thick outline and an offset, in a color with at least 3:1 contrast against every background it sits on. Override it per component only when a background requires it.
to the height of your sticky header and footer, and make sure cookie banners can't cover the element that has focus.

Put the mouse away and walk each page with Tab and Shift+Tab. Every stop needs a visible, uncovered ring. Repeat once in forced colors mode, using a Windows contrast theme or the forced-colors emulation in your browser's DevTools.
